transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Ravi (Redwood Infra Eng), Sofia (Redwood SRE), Ben (ClearSight ML), Priya (ClearSight Infra), Diego (ClearSight SRE), Ava (ClearSight Data Platform), Tom (Product Owner)

Summary (auto):
Customer sees intermittent OOMs and timeouts in staging; failures manifest as cudaMemcpy OOM, occasional dmesg OOM-killer logs, and grpc stream resets during high-batch spikes. Discussion covered root causes (memory fragmentation, batching spikes, KV cache pressure), retry/backoff semantics, and mitigations (quantization, batch sizing, pre-warming, memory accounting). Next steps: collect support bundle, run repro, try quantized model, assess Dedicated capacity.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'll hand off to Jordan and then we can jump straight into the logs you shared.
[00:12] Ben: yeah thanks. appreciate it. the failure was pretty noisy in staging overnight so, uh, we're hoping to get concrete next steps.
[00:20] Jordan: cool. quick intros — I'm Jordan, SE on runtime. Ravi's from our infra team, Sofia does reliability. can you kick off with what you saw, Ben?
[00:30] Ben: sure. so, gist: when we ramp to ~1800 rps with 4s average seq len we start seeing OOMs on the GPU workers. logs show "cudaMemcpy failed: out of memory" then some requests time out, grpc streams reset. sometimes process disappears and dmesg shows "oom-killer invoked". it's intermittent, not a deterministic repro.
[00:54] Priya: i think worth adding — this is in the customer's VPC with our private deployment. we have nvidia-driver 535 and the CUDA 12 stack, pods are p3-like (A100) in on-prem colo. we limit container memory with cgroups, but kernel OOMs still happen.
[01:12] Jordan: okay. thanks. a few hypotheses: (1) memory fragmentation over long-running processes + KV cache exacerbates peak memory usage on batch spikes; (2) batching config leads to occasional very large internal batches due to bursty arrivals; (3) quantization or model offload behavior causing async allocations; (4) CUDA driver/runtime/oom-killer interplay with pinned memory.
[01:36] Diego: yep we saw kv-cache grow over time on hot routes; we were using a large prefix cache with few eviction rules. when traffic hits a new long context it pulls big kv segments.
[01:48] Sofia: question — are you using continuous batching or fixed window?
[01:52] Ben: continuous batching, with max_batch_size 32 and target latency 120ms. we've been tuning but seems like during load tests spikes create 64-like effective batches because multiple models share the same worker pool.
[02:05] Ravi: that shared worker pool is an important detail. if two model variants use the same GPU pool, an aggregate batch can oversubscribe memory. on our side we also saw ephemeral spikes when KV cache population and a large batch co-occur.
[02:18] Jordan: exactly. pragmatic mitigations: 1) enforce stricter max_batch_size per model and per-worker; 2) introduce per-model memory quotas within the pool (soft limits + eviction); 3) tighter KV cache eviction policy — limit total KV bytes per worker; 4) add pre-warm traffic pattern / steady background keepalive to avoid large cold allocations.
[02:43] Ben: can you explain the memory accounting — we thought GPU memory comes from the model + activations + kv cache + batching scratch. does Redwood track all of that and prevent oversub?
[02:54] Jordan: we track allocations at runtime but there are two tricky things: fragmentation and external pinned host buffers used for cudaMemcpy. fragmentation can make a free 4GB slab non-contiguous for a future allocation; pinned buffers for IO can also reduce available GPU memory. we report headroom but in edge cases the driver returns OOM.
[03:12] Priya: we also saw timeouts with streaming responses. some clients abort mid-stream and then a retry floods the system. our retry policy is simple immediate retry — that compounded the problem.
[03:24] Maya: good point — retry semantics matter. our recommended pattern is idempotent requests where possible plus exponential backoff with jitter and server-side limits. Jordan, can you walk through how Redwood handles retries now?
[03:34] Jordan: sure. by default Redwood's hosted runtime will retry transient RPC failures up to configurable N, with exponential backoff and jitter. for private deployments the same logic applies but customers can override at load-balancer/proxy. we also implement request deduplication in the request-id path for some routes to avoid duplicate execution, but not all endpoints are idempotent — streaming generation is tough.
[03:55] Diego: so streaming plus immediate client retries = double work and more batches. we need guidance to make clients back off more gracefully.
[04:03] Sofia: also consider circuit breakers on the worker pool — if the pool trips due to memory pressure, fail fast and route to a lower-capacity replica or queued mode.
[04:12] Priya: is there a way to detect when a pending batch will exceed memory before we accept it?
[04:18] Jordan: yes — we have a pre-check that estimates memory based on sequence length distribution and KV size. it returns 'accept', 'delay', or 'reject' depending on available headroom. that pre-check uses conservative estimates; seems like in your setup it wasn't sufficient due to shared pool aggregation.
[04:34] Ben: we also saw kernel driver messages about CUDA launch failures like "CUDA error 700: an illegal instruction was encountered" — is that consistent with OOMs or a separate problem?
[04:43] Ravi: often those are separate, can be driver mismatch or subtle nondeterminism; but if address space is corrupted due to OOM or improper stream handling you can get weird errors. worth capturing full coredump/gpu backtrace.
[04:58] Maya: okay let's go through the logs you sent earlier — Jordan?
[05:01] Jordan: i pulled the snippet. at 02:17:44 we see request-id 0x7ab3, worker-12: "cudaMalloc failed: out of memory" then 30s later multiple GRPC stream resets. preceding that at 02:17:30 you can see a KV cache refill event increased memory footprint by ~1.6GB. so correlation is strong.
[05:22] Ben: yeah that's one of the examples. sometimes it recovers after a few minutes, other times the process is gone and kube restarts it.
[05:30] Priya: and we have cgroup memory set to 64GB per container; A100 has 80GB. bash dmesg shows OOM killer choosing process with the highest RSS — so obviously memory exceeded system thresholds.
[05:44] Jordan: couple low-friction changes: reduce max_batch_size to 16, set per-model kv-cache cap to 8GB, enable eviction to LRU with TTL of 10 minutes for inactive contexts. also enable redis-based shared KV cache across workers so single worker doesn't blow up on cold traffic.
[06:02] Ben: shared KV cache? curious — doesn't that add network hop latency?
[06:07] Jordan: yes small tradeoff. we provide an optional remote KV store optimized for hot keys with async fetch that reduces per-worker memory. in practice it adds ~10-20ms for cold prefixes but removes big memory spikes.
[06:18] Ava: is that available for private deployments?
[06:21] Jordan: yes, we can deploy a local Redis/rocksdb cluster inside the VPC/on-prem with accelerated path and local cache. it's part of the Private runtime pattern.
[06:30] Priya: what about quantization — we were thinking of moving to 8-bit to reduce memory. any caveats?
[06:35] Ravi: quant helps both memory and compute but can change sampling behavior and sometimes increases CPU pre/post processing. we recommend a canary: quantize on staging, validate evals for quality drift, then enable for low-latency paths.
[06:46] Jordan: specifically, for your model we expect ~35-40% GPU memory reduction with dynamic 8-bit quantization, but activations still scale with sequence length. quantization also reduces the size of KV items proportionally if you quantize KV tensors.
[06:58] Ben: there's also noise: some quantized kernels allocate extra workspace that can cause fragmentation unless the runtime uses a workspace pool. does Redwood have workspace pooling?
[07:08] Jordan: yes we do. we have a configurable workspace allocator to reuse scratch space across inferences. that reduces fragmentation. but if you have mixed runs (quant + FP16) the allocator needs to be tuned.
[07:20] Tom: at the business level — if this continues what's the suggested route: Dedicated capacity? more headroom?
[07:26] Maya: two paths: short term you tune batching/KV and retry, quantize where possible. mid-term, consider Dedicated capacity with reserve headroom or vertical scaling. Dedicated gives predictability and isolation which prevents noisy neighbors.
[07:40] Priya: we have reasons to prefer private deployment (compliance) so scaling horizontally is limited by colo capacity. can Redwood suggest guardrails we can enforce in our autoscaler?
[07:50] Jordan: recommend autoscale with memory-aware policies: scale up when average headroom < 20% for N minutes, don't scale down if KV refill rate high, and maintain a reserve pool for cold-starts. also use per-pod admission control to limit batch sizes.
[08:06] Diego: what about retry semantics again? our current client retries immediately on stream reset and that spikes the system.
[08:12] Jordan: add exponential backoff (base 200ms with factor 2 and jitter up to 300ms) and cap client-side retries to 2 for streaming. server-side we can provide 429-based throttling with Retry-After headers so clients don't react with blind retries.
[08:27] Ben: sending Retry-After will be great. do you also support queueing?
[08:31] Sofia: we have a queueing mode that accepts request metadata and returns a ticket — useful when latency SLOs can't be met. it's opt-in and good for high-throughput batch workloads.
[08:39] Priya: ok. i want to make sure we get the diagnostic artifacts right. what exactly do you need us to collect?
[08:45] Jordan: at minimum: (1) runtime logs around failure windows (timestamps, request-ids), (2) output of nvidia-smi -q -x during the failure and before, (3) dmesg around OOM killer lines, (4) container cgroup mem.stat and kernel OOM logs, (5) sample pprof heap/stack traces if possible, (6) our support-bundle script will capture grpc traces. we'll share the script.
[09:08] Ben: ok we'll run that next window and upload.
[09:12] Priya: what about the process disappear cases — sometimes we see segfault in core but no evidence in logs. do you recommend core dumps?
[09:19] Ravi: yes enable core_pattern and capture GPU backtraces. we can help parse them. also consider setting the driver to more verbose cuda logging.
[09:29] Jordan: one more advanced mitigation: graceful eviction of KV cache when memory pressure is detected. instead of hard OOM, runtime can proactively trim KV entries to free memory for active batches. we can enable that behavior in your runtime build.
[09:44] Ben: that sounds promising. is there a tradeoff in QoL for the user? i.e., will trimmed contexts cause degraded answers?
[09:49] Jordan: yes — trimming cold prefixes can cause quality regressions for requests that rely on long context history. but we can do LRU with heuristics favoring active users and preserve last N turns. it's tunable.
[09:58] Diego: about driver/cuda errors — we saw cuda error 700 sometimes. any pattern?
[10:03] Jordan: often driver-level errors point to hardware or driver mismatch; but in our experience, memory corruption after an OOM or concurrent cudaMemcpy from multiple threads without proper stream synchronization can surface as 700. capturing GPU stacktrace is essential.
[10:18] Priya: one question from our security team — are support bundles safe to share? do they contain PII or payloads?
[10:24] Maya: good call. our support script strips request payloads by default and only collects metadata and logs, but we'll give a sanitized mode. we can also run under NDA-protected channel.
[10:36] Ben: will you share recommended config JSON for batching and kv cache?
[10:40] Jordan: yes — we'll send a suggested policy: max_batch_size=16, concurrency_per_gpu=4, kv_cache_limit_per_worker=8GB, kv_eviction_ttl=10m, workspace_pool_enabled=true, retry_headers with 429.
[10:52] Ava: any suggestion for monitoring dashboards?
[10:56] Sofia: track free_gpu_mem, kv_cache_bytes, batch_size_distribution, queue_length, retry_rate, stream_resets, and per-request p90/p99 tail latency. set alerts on free_gpu_mem < 15% and retry_rate spike > 5% of requests.
[11:12] Ben: okay this is actionable. question — if we decide to move more to 8-bit, what's the typical rollout plan?
[11:18] Jordan: do a canary: deploy quantized model for 5% traffic in staging, run eval prompts and production-like workloads, compare embeddings / sampling / hallucination rates. if pass, ramp 25% then 100%. also run load tests to profile memory.
[11:31] Priya: final item, can Redwood run a joint smoke test with us where you generate load and we collect traces?
[11:36] Maya: yes we can do a co-run. we'll coordinate with Ben and Priya and book the deep infra session for the week of 2026-06-22.
[11:44] Ben: great. thanks.
[11:46] Tom: quick business note — if we need Dedicated to get predictable latency we'll probably want a 3-month pilot, pricing details appreciated.
[11:53] Maya: noted. i'll send pricing and the pilot template after the call.
[11:58] Jordan: final technical note — for your case I'd prioritize: 1) stricter per-worker admission control 2) kv cache caps + eviction 3) try quantization in staging 4) adjust client retry backoff 5) collect support bundle and schedule follow-up.
[12:11] Ben: good summary. we'll run the bundle and pick a time. thanks all.

End of transcript.
